title: Feather and fan lap throw
subtitle: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw in the classic 18-stitch feather-and-fan repeat, DK.
excerpt: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw worked flat in feather-and-fan stitch (also called old shale), a classic scalloped lace that uses yarn-overs and decreases in an 18-stitch, 4-row repeat. About 700 g of DK.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 2nd series (1886), §Old Shale or Feather Stitch, documents the 18-stitch, 4-row feather-and-fan pattern as a traditional Shetland shawl stitch adapted for domestic blankets. Mary Thomas's Book of Knitting Patterns (1943), §Old Shale, gives the same repeat with alternative 12 and 24-stitch versions.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 28 rows = 10 × 10 cm in feather-and-fan pattern on 4 mm needles, unblocked.

stitchCountCheckpoints.label: Halfway check — 216 sts (multiple of 18), about 60 cm

glossaryTerms.definition: A traditional knitting stitch originating in Shetland. The four-row repeat alternates a plain knit row, a purl row, and a patterned row that places clusters of yarn-overs to form fans separated by clusters of decreases that form the chevron points. The resulting fabric has scalloped edges and undulating columns across the width.

Inserting the right needle through three stitches at once and knitting them as a single stitch, reducing the stitch count by two. Used in feather-and-fan to create the sharp decrease points between fan sections.

Single-panel construction; no seaming. Feather-and-fan was chosen because its yarn-over-and-decrease structure produces a naturally scalloped cast-on and cast-off edge, eliminating the need for a separate border treatment. The pattern is worked in a simple four-row repeat: two plain rows and two patterned rows. Budget about 700 g (about 1,540 m / 1,680 yards) of DK. Buy in matched dye lots. The scalloped edges make this a particularly good gift blanket.

content.text: 22 stitches and 28 rows to 10 cm in feather-and-fan pattern on 4 mm needles. Feather-and-fan rows are slightly taller than stocking-stitch rows. Swatch the full 4-row, 18-stitch repeat for at least 12 cm.
If your row gauge is 26 rows per 10 cm instead of 28, the same row count produces the throw about 9 cm longer. Target 120 cm by measuring with tape, not by counting rows.
Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 216 stitches (a multiple of 18 for the feather-and-fan repeat). Long-tail tail: (4 × 216) / 10 + 15 = 86.4 + 15 = 101 cm. Measure 120 cm of tail.
Row 3 (RS): *k3tog, (yo, k1) six times, yo, k3tog; repeat from * to end. Count: each 18-stitch repeat starts with 18 stitches and ends with 18 stitches.
Repeat rows 1 to 4 until the throw measures 120 cm. When you set this aside, note which of the four rows is next.

At row 168 (about 60 cm): count across. You should have 216 stitches. The k3tog removes 2 stitches; the 7 yo in the same repeat add 7 stitches; net change is +5, but k3tog counts as 3 removed and 1 remaining, count after a plain row 1 or 2, not after row 3. At row 334 (about 119 cm): count after a plain row before casting off.
Repeat count off by one stitch: a yo was skipped or added. The six-yo-plus-one sequence in row 3 is seven yarn-overs total; count them as you place each one in the first few repeats.
Scallop peaks irregular in size: k3tog was worked as k2tog in some repeats. Confirm three stitches are on the needle before each decrease point.
End on row 1 or 2 (plain row). Cast off knitwise with a relaxed tension. The scalloped edge of the cast-off will mirror the cast-on edge if the throw ends on row 4 of a complete repeat.
Weave in both ends. Wet block the finished throw to open the yarn-overs and define the scallop shapes: wet, pin each scallop peak at the cast-on and cast-off edges, leave to dry fully.
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle for superwash DK. Lay flat to dry, reshaping the scallop edges. Non-superwash wool: hand wash in cool water.

From feather-and-fan, try a multi-colour version. Work two or three colours in garter-stitch stripes of four rows each. Use feather-and-fan rows within each stripe. Each colour change falls on a WS garter row, keeping the join clean.
